newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cen bank signals T-bill rates to stay low.
newsitem.headline: Russian cen bank signals T-bill rates to stay low.

text.p: Russia's central bank made it clear to the markets that record low yields on domestic government securities were here to stay when it announced on Friday it would lower its key refinancing rate.

Fixed income analysts said the move reflected improved Russian fundamentals though they said a correction and slightly higher yields driven by domestic operators could push yields, which fell below 20 percent on Friday, up as far as the low 20s.

The central bank said it would lower the refinancing rate to 24 percent from 36 percent from June 16, nudging the 20 percent at which the rate was introduced in 1991, and which held until March 1992, soon after economic reforms were launched.

The bank does not operate a formal refinancing facility charged at the refinancing rate, but the refinancing rate is used in many contracts and T-bill yields have only gone above the rate once, during the 1996 presidential election campaign.

"The move is very important," Credit Suisse Asset Management fund manager Jana Benesova said. "You cannot use the refinancing rate actively, but some of the shorter maturity loans are derived from it. It is definitely a positive indicator."
Prices of bills in secondary trade rose immediately upon news of the cut, especially for six month and longer paper.

A six-month bill maturing December 10 rose to 91.85 at close, off a high of 92.45, from 91.04 at the close on Tuesday, the previous day of trade. Its yield fell to 17.99 from 19.63. A month ago average market yields were in the high 20s.
The bank gave no reason for the cuts, which follow a sharp fall in Treasury bill yields, a strengthening rouble and a steady decline in the inflation rate.
"We may see a correction," Benesova said. "But not from fundamentals, which are good."
Foreigners choosing between emerging markets would still choose Russia where rates are relatively high compared to its credit rating, but domestic operators may push yields up temporarily, she said.

Gas group Gazprom, which has a large T-bill portfolio and needs to raise trillions of roubles to pay taxes by June 20, and banks which may sell bills to increase cash positions ahead of end-of-quarter accounts, could lead prices lower, analysts said.
The Finance Ministry will auction 20 trillion roubles of bonds and bills next week, the largest sum ever.
It must raise about 8.4 trillion roubles to pay maturing issues and will offer some bonds as part of a voluntary plan for holders to replace non-tax-liable bonds with taxable bonds.
But a fixed income analyst at a Moscow bank said the new refinancing rate was a belated recognition of market levels rather than a strong new signal.

"It ratifies market moves that have already happened. There seems to be plenty of (capital) inflow at these levels," the analyst said, pointing to strong fundamentals and predicting the market would generally be stable.
